blocks.content: Tell me about yourself opened the interview with a structured narrative. Why are you leaving is another near universal question, and one of the trickiest to answer well, since it requires being honest about a genuine reason for moving on, without badmouthing your current or former company in the process.

This question matters because how you talk about a past or current employer is a real, direct preview of how you might talk about this new company one day, if things ever end here too. Interviewers are listening closely for professionalism, not just the literal content of the reason.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024893121-817307584.png
blocks.alt: Why are you leaving covers answering honestly about your reason for moving on without badmouthing your current company

blocks.content: 1. What Interviewers Are Actually Listening For
blocks.text: 1. What Interviewers Are Actually Listening For

blocks.content: A few specific things get evaluated here. Whether you speak professionally about a past or current employer, even when there were genuinely difficult aspects of that experience. Whether the reason given reflects genuine self awareness, a real understanding of what you are looking for, not just a reaction to something negative.

And whether the reason connects logically to this new role, since a reason that has nothing to do with what this specific opportunity actually offers can leave an interviewer wondering if you are just looking for any exit rather than this particular opportunity.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024895192-145523972.png
blocks.alt: Interviewers listen for professional tone about your current employer, genuine self awareness in the reason, and a logical connection to this new role

blocks.content: 2. Badmouthing Versus Honest, Professional Framing

Badmouthing your current company or manager, even when the underlying frustration is genuinely valid, tends to make an interviewer quietly wonder how you might describe their own company in a similar conversation somewhere else down the line.

Honest, professional framing of a genuine reason, one that focuses on what you are looking for rather than what specifically went wrong, reads as mature and trustworthy, even when the underlying situation being described was genuinely difficult.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024896783-712721498.png
blocks.alt: Badmouthing a current employer makes an interviewer wonder how you would describe them later; honest, professional framing reads as mature and trustworthy

blocks.content: {"headers":["Badmouthing Framing","Honest, Professional Framing"],"rows":[["My manager never gave me real ownership","I am looking for a role with more ownership over technical direction"],["The company has poor engineering culture","I am looking for an environment with stronger engineering practices"],["My team was disorganized and slow","I am looking for a team with clearer processes and faster decision making"]]}
3. A Worked Example
A concrete story shows this framing applied well. A genuine desire for more ownership over technical direction than the current role allowed was the real underlying reason for looking to move on.

First person quote: "I genuinely wanted more ownership over technical direction than my current role allows. I framed my answer around what I am actually looking for, rather than what is wrong with my current company, since the company itself has been a reasonable place to work. I named the specific gap honestly, the lack of real ownership over direction, without complaint or criticism attached to it. And I connected it directly to why this new role specifically offers exactly that kind of ownership, which is genuinely what drew me to apply."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024898311-649646307.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: framing around what is being sought rather than what is wrong, naming the specific gap honestly, and connecting it directly to the new role

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Criticizing a current manager or company directly, by name or specific detail, even when the criticism feels justified. This tends to make an interviewer quietly concerned about how you might describe their company in a future conversation.
4. A Simple Reframing Technique

A genuinely useful technique for this question. State what you are looking for, not what you are running from, since framing the reason around a positive pull toward something is far more professional than framing it around a negative push away from something.

Keep the tone factual and specific, not emotional or vague, since specificity reads as genuine self reflection while vagueness or emotional language can read as either evasive or unresolved. And connect the reason directly to this specific new opportunity, showing the move is deliberate, not just an exit from something uncomfortable.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024899909-695530967.png
blocks.alt: A simple reframing technique: state what you are looking for rather than running from, keep the tone factual and specific, and connect it to this new opportunity

blocks.content: 5. Genuine Versus Generic Reasons

A generic, vague reason that could genuinely apply to almost any move, looking for new challenges, wanting to grow, feels hollow and unconvincing, since it does not actually reveal anything specific about your real situation or motivation.

A specific, genuine reason tied to your own actual situation, more ownership, a different technical focus, a specific kind of environment, feels credible and thought through, since it demonstrates real self awareness about what you actually want, not just a safe, generic answer.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024901456-163902192.png
blocks.alt: A generic, vague reason feels hollow; a specific, genuine reason tied to your real situation feels credible and thought through

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A specific reason tied to your own real situation is almost always more convincing than a safe, generic one, even though specificity can feel slightly more exposing to share.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine this answer. Criticizing a current manager or company directly, by name or specific detail, which tends to raise real concern about future professionalism. Giving a reason so vague it sounds evasive, leaving the interviewer without a genuine sense of what is actually motivating the move.
And giving a reason with no clear connection to the new role, which can leave an interviewer wondering if you are simply looking for any exit rather than this specific opportunity.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024903027-384100553.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: criticizing a current employer directly, giving a reason so vague it sounds evasive, and no connection to the new role

blocks.content: 7. Preparing Your Own Why Are You Leaving Answer
blocks.text: 7. Preparing Your Own Why Are You Leaving Answer

blocks.content: Identify the genuine, specific reason behind your own move, then reframe it around what you are looking for rather than what is wrong with your current situation, keeping the tone factual and free of complaint.

The strongest answers here are specific and honest about the real gap being addressed, while remaining genuinely professional about the current or past employer, since both halves together are what this question is actually testing for.
This question is judged less on the reason itself, and more on how professionally you describe it.
8. Weaker Signal Versus Stronger Signal

9. Common Mistakes

["Naming specific negative incidents at the current company: reads as unprofessional regardless of how valid the underlying complaint was.","Giving a reason so generic it could apply to any move at all: feels hollow and unconvincing to a listening interviewer.","Leaving the reason disconnected from why this specific role fits: raises doubt about whether this is a deliberate, specific move."]
items: Naming specific negative incidents at the current company: reads as unprofessional regardless of how valid the underlying complaint was.
Giving a reason so generic it could apply to any move at all: feels hollow and unconvincing to a listening interviewer.
Leaving the reason disconnected from why this specific role fits: raises doubt about whether this is a deliberate, specific move.
